title: Alexander Drinks the Suspect Medicine
text:
In 333 BC, as Alexander the Great marched through Cilicia toward the Persian king Darius, he fell dangerously ill. Some said he caught a chill bathing in the icy river Cydnus. According to Plutarch, his physicians thought the case so desperate that none dared treat him, fearing the anger of the Macedonians if he died in their care.

Only Philip of Acarnania, an old friend, agreed to try a strong purge. Just then a letter arrived from the general Parmenion warning Alexander that Philip had been bribed by Darius to poison him, with money and the promise of the king's daughter in marriage. Alexander read it and slipped it under his pillow without showing it to anyone.

When Philip came in with the cup, Alexander handed him the letter and drank the medicine while Philip read. Plutarch describes the scene: the king calm and cheerful, the doctor horrified, raising his hands to heaven and begging Alexander to trust him. The drug at first left Alexander weak and nearly speechless, but Philip nursed him back, and within days he showed himself to his army again. Arrian tells the same story.
lesson: When you have good reason to trust someone, show it openly at the moment it counts. Visible confidence can bind people to you more firmly than suspicion protects you.
people: Alexander the Great, Philip of Acarnania, Parmenion
source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 19; Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 2.4
